opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a real opportunity there, though I'd frame it a bit carefully. The general-purpose models have gotten remarkably good at medical reasoning: answering clinical questions, summarizing literature, even interpreting some kinds of imaging. So the question isn't "do you need your own model to do medicine?" It's more "what does your organization's data let you do that a general model can't?"

Healthcare organizations sit on enormous amounts of longitudinal data: years of patient records, lab results, imaging, notes from clinicians, outcomes. That's incredibly valuable, because it captures the specifics of a patient population, local practice patterns, and the way a particular health system documents things. A model that has seen that data can be much better at tasks like predicting which patients are likely to deteriorate, flagging things in a chart a busy clinician might miss, or just drafting notes in the style and format that system actually uses.

I don't think most organizations should train a model from scratch, though. That's expensive and usually unnecessary. The more practical path is to start from a strong base model and adapt it: fine-tuning, retrieval over your own records, or some combination, so you get the broad medical knowledge plus the local specifics. That's also nicer from a privacy standpoint, because you can keep the sensitive data inside your own environment and adapt the model there rather than shipping patient data around.

The hard parts are less about the modeling and more about everything around it. Data is often messy and fragmented across systems. You need rigorous evaluation, ideally prospective, in real clinical workflows, not just retrospective benchmarks. And you have to think about bias. If your historical data reflects disparities in care, a model trained on it can perpetuate them unless you're deliberate about it.

But if you get those pieces right, I think the payoff is big. Clinicians spend a huge fraction of their time on documentation and information retrieval, and a model that really understands your system's data could give a lot of that time back to actual patient care. That's one of the areas I'm most excited about.

r001.rationale: It says a model adapted to an organization’s longitudinal records can perform better on organization-specific tasks than a general-purpose model, which lacks those local details.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's actually a really exciting area, but I'd frame it a little differently than "bespoke models trained from scratch." What we've seen over and over is that general-purpose models trained on a very broad distribution of data end up being surprisingly good at specialized domains, and the gains from starting over with only your own data are usually smaller than people expect. The medical knowledge in a large general model is already pretty substantial. What a healthcare organization actually has that's unique is context: their patient population, their workflows, their formulary, the way their clinicians write notes, the particular ways things go wrong in their system.

So the opportunity is really about adapting a strong base model to that context rather than building something from the ground up. That might be fine-tuning on de-identified records, or it might be retrieval over the organization's own guidelines and prior cases, or it might be something as simple as a well-constructed system that pulls the right pieces of the chart into the model at the right time. A lot of the value is in the plumbing, honestly. Getting a model to see the longitudinal history of a patient, lab trends over years, imaging alongside the notes, rather than one isolated snippet.

The other thing I'd say is that the data in these organizations is messy and much smaller than people think once you filter for quality. So the base model doing the heavy lifting matters a lot. Where you really do want organization-specific training is in things like the local coding conventions, the specific device outputs, the kinds of multimodal data a hospital generates that aren't well represented on the public web. Pathology slides, certain kinds of imaging, time series from monitors. Those are areas where a general model has seen very little and where your own data is genuinely differentiating.

And then there's the trust and validation piece, which I think is underappreciated. A model that's been evaluated against your own patient population, with your clinicians in the loop looking at where it's wrong, is one you can actually deploy. That evaluation loop is probably more valuable than the training itself. So I'd say: start with the best general model you can get, adapt it with your context, and invest heavily in measuring how it does on your actual cases. That's where the real leverage is.

r001.rationale: The response says organization-specific training is valuable where public models lack local conventions or specialized data, and recommends adapting a strong base model to that context—suggesting it can perform better for the organization’s needs.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of opportunity there, because healthcare organizations have data that reflects their particular patients, their workflows, and the kinds of care they provide. If you can combine that with the capabilities of a broadly trained model, you could build something that’s much more useful in that particular setting.

I wouldn’t necessarily think of it as training a whole model from scratch on an organization’s data. It might be adapting a model, or giving it access to the relevant information at the right time. For example, helping a clinician understand a patient’s history before a visit could be very valuable.

The important thing is to demonstrate that it actually works in that environment. Does it improve care? Does it save clinicians time? Does it work well across different patient populations? And you need to do all of that while protecting patient privacy. So I’m excited about the potential, but the evaluation and the way you integrate it into clinical practice are just as important as the model itself.

r001.rationale: The response says combining an organization’s patient and workflow data with a broadly trained model could make it much more useful in that setting, communicating potential improvement over a general model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a pretty significant opportunity there. Every healthcare organization has data that reflects its patient population, its clinical practices, and the systems it uses. Being able to adapt a model to that environment could make it much more useful.

I wouldn’t necessarily assume you want to train a model from scratch on just that organization’s data, though. You probably want to start with a model that has broad capabilities and medical knowledge, and then adapt it, or give it access to relevant local information. Some things belong in the model’s training, and some things are better retrieved when you need them.

The important question is whether that actually improves care. Can you help clinicians find the information they need, reduce administrative work, or identify something that might otherwise get missed? You need careful evaluation on the population you’re serving, strong privacy protections, and a clear sense of when the system should defer to a clinician. But I think the potential to make expertise more accessible is really exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says organization-specific data or information could make a model more useful, but it does not clearly say that training on nonpublic data may outperform a general model trained on public data; it also presents retrieval as an alternative to training.
